forces: Mixed chorus, baritone solo, orchestra and organ
performers: Bernard Kruysen, baritone; Chorale Philippe Caillard; Orchestre national de l’Opéra de Monte-Carlo, Louis Frémaux
question: How does a gentle Requiem make room for the day of wrath?
intro: The Libera me is the oldest music in the Requiem and the only place where judgement breaks in. Hear a baritone over plucked basses, a fortissimo “Dies irae”, a sudden calm, and the opening prayer returning in the whole choir.

cues.title: A plucked, steady bass
cues.text: Cellos and basses pluck a steady pattern of two quarter notes, a rest and an upbeat, while the organ holds long notes beneath. The baritone enters on “Libera me, Domine” with a wide-ranging melody and some sharp leaps.
cues.evidence: Page 92 of the score marks the cello and bass parts pizz. over organ pedal, with the baritone entering in the third bar. The report’s onset density is 6.8 per second at 0:05 and 0:25, consistent with a plucked repeated pattern. Wikipedia’s description gives the rhythm and the baritone’s wide range.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The oldest music in the Requiem
cues.text: Fauré wrote the Libera me in 1877 as a separate baritone piece, the year he became choirmaster at the Madeleine. He added it to the Requiem only in 1890, so it is the earliest music in the work.
cues.evidence: The Wikipedia article on the Requiem gives 1877 for the independent Libera me and 1890 for its addition to the Requiem; IRCAM’s biography of Fauré gives his appointment as maître de chapelle at the Madeleine in 1877.

cues.title: The choir takes up the text
cues.text: At about 1:10 the choir continues the text with “Tremens factus sum ego” (“I am made to tremble”), in four parts moving together, pianissimo. The baritone’s leaping line gives way to hushed chords; the level drops to one of the quietest points before the Dies irae.
cues.evidence: The report finds a boundary at 1:10 (0.30) and level falling from −17.1 dB at 1:05 to −25.4 dB at 1:15. Page 97 of the score (letter C) marks the choir’s pp chordal entry; Wikipedia’s description gives the four-part homophony. The baritone’s separate staff rests from here until page 112.

cues.title: Faster, with horns
cues.text: The tempo quickens to Più mosso, and fortissimo horn chords break in around 1:35. “Dies illa, dies irae” follows in fortissimo from the choir alone, with trombones joining the horns in repeated chords.
cues.evidence: Relative level rises from −14.6 dB at 1:30 to −8.8 dB at 1:35, with boundaries at 1:46 (0.39) and 1:52 (0.38). Pages 99–101 of the score mark Più mosso, ff horn chords and, at letter E, trombone chords; the trumpet staff and the baritone’s staff are empty.

cues.title: The Dies irae, briefly
cues.text: Fauré left out the long Dies irae sequence, but its words surface here. The sleeve note by Louis Aubert says it passes “as an indispensable episode”, with none of the grandiloquent or macabre effects of other Requiems.
cues.evidence: The scanned Erato sleeve reads, in French, “Le Dies irae y passe comme un épisode indispensable”, and says the Fauré Requiem has no grandiloquent or macabre effects. The Wikipedia article on the Requiem says Fauré set only the Pie Jesu section of the sequence.

cues.title: Wrath gives way to prayer
cues.text: At about 2:20 the fortissimo stops and the choir sings “Requiem aeternam dona eis” piano, marked dolce, in the same rhythmic motion. The level falls by about ten decibels in five seconds as judgement turns to prayer.
cues.evidence: Relative level falls from −4.1 dB at 2:20 to −13.8 dB at 2:25, with a boundary at 2:20 (0.67). Page 102 of the score (letter F) marks the choir p dolce after the ff of pages 100–101.

cues.title: A text the liturgy dropped
cues.text: The Roman Missal of 1962 still contained the Dies irae. In 1969–70, Archbishop Annibale Bugnini explained, the reformers removed “Libera me, Domine” and the Dies irae among texts that overstressed judgement, fear and despair.
cues.evidence: The “Use in the Roman liturgy” section of the Wikipedia article on the Dies irae gives the 1962 Missal as the last edition before the reforms and quotes Bugnini on the 1969–70 removal of “Libera me, Domine” and the Dies irae.

cues.title: The ostinato returns first
cues.text: At about 2:52 the tempo returns to Moderato and the plucked ostinato of the opening restarts, with a quiet repeated rhythm in the timpani, while the choir finishes “luceat eis”. The first melody has not yet come back; the pulse returns before the tune.
cues.evidence: The report finds a boundary at 2:52 (0.62) and onset density rising from 1.2 per second at 2:50 to 3.0 at 3:00. Page 105 of the score (letter H, Moderato) shows pizzicato strings and repeated notes in the timpani staff under the choir’s last “luceat eis”.

cues.title: The opening melody, in unison
cues.text: About nine bars later, near 3:10, the whole choir sings the opening melody, “Libera me, Domine”, in unison. The timpani’s regular pulse breaks into isolated notes, the strings keep their repeated chords, and quiet horn and trombone chords pass beneath.
cues.evidence: Pages 105–107 of the score give nine bars of the ostinato after letter H and then the unison “Libera me” on page 107, where the timpani continue only as isolated notes and rests on pages 107–109. At about two seconds a bar this puts the entry near 3:10, where the report’s onset density dips to 0.8 per second. Wikipedia’s description says the choir repeats the baritone’s opening statement in unison.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A long crescendo
cues.text: From about 3:36 the choir sings “Quando caeli movendi sunt et terra” (“when heaven and earth are moved”) in a long crescendo to the loudest late stretch, around 3:50 to 4:05, then a diminuendo. The strings keep the same repeated chords.
cues.evidence: Relative level rises from −13.4 dB at 3:35 to −6.0 dB at 3:50 and −5.0 dB at 3:55, then falls to −13.2 dB at 4:10; boundaries at 3:36 (0.28) and 3:50 (0.40). Pages 109–111 of the score (letters K and L) mark cresc., f and dim. with the strings in repeated chords.

cues.title: The baritone alone again
cues.text: Near 4:14 the baritone sings “Libera me, Domine, de morte aeterna” once more, alone over repeated pianissimo chords, and the choir answers pianissimo. The movement ends where it began, but quietly.
cues.evidence: The report finds a boundary at 4:14 (0.44), with level falling from −13.2 dB at 4:10 to −21.3 dB at 4:15 and onset density of 6.4 per second at 4:20 and 5.8 at 4:25. Pages 112–113 of the score give the baritone’s solo, after his long rest, and the choir’s closing “Libera me, Domine”.

cues.title: A held chord, decaying
cues.text: In the last bars the choir’s soft “Libera me, Domine” gives way to a bowed chord held under a fermata. Listen to the decay: the file’s level falls to about −35 dB by 4:50.
cues.evidence: Relative level falls from −22.7 dB at 4:45 to −35.1 dB at 4:50. Page 113 of the score marks the final strings arco with fermatas.

transitions.title: The baritone yields to the choir
transitions.how: The baritone’s melody finishes its text, and at letter C the choir takes over with “Tremens factus sum ego” pianissimo, in four parts moving together. The plucked ostinato gives way to quiet strings, and the level falls. Fauré passes the same prayer from one voice to many, and from a leaping melody to a hushed chord progression, so the fear of the text is carried by the group, not by the soloist, who now rests for a long stretch.
transitions.evidence: The report finds a boundary at 1:10 (0.30) and level falling from −17.1 dB at 1:05 to −25.4 dB at 1:15. Pages 96–97 of the score show the baritone’s last phrase, the choir’s pp entry at letter C and the strings changing from pizzicato to arco.

transitions.title: Crescendo, faster tempo, brass
transitions.how: The choir’s quiet entries crescendo through letter D on “dum discussio venerit” (“when judgement comes”). At the end of the page the tempo changes from Moderato to Più mosso, and fortissimo horn chords break in. “Dies illa, dies irae” then comes in repeated forte chords from the whole choir, with horns and trombones. The change is made by tempo, volume and the sudden arrival of brass, not by a new melody.
transitions.evidence: Relative level rises from −14.6 dB at 1:30 to −8.8 dB at 1:35, with boundaries at 1:46 (0.39) and 1:52 (0.38). Pages 98–101 of the score give the crescendo at letter D, the Più mosso marking and the horn and trombone staves in use.

transitions.title: Fortissimo drops to piano
transitions.how: The fortissimo chords of “Dies illa” stop, and at letter F the choir sings “Requiem aeternam dona eis” piano and dolce, in the same rhythmic motion as the wrath it follows. The brass drop to piano and the strings continue with softer repeated chords. Fauré turns judgement into prayer without changing the pulse: only the dynamics, the voices’ colour and the words change.
transitions.evidence: Relative level falls from −4.1 dB at 2:20 to −13.8 dB at 2:25, with a boundary at 2:20 (0.67). Page 102 of the score marks letter F, the choir p dolce and the horns marked dolce.

transitions.title: The first pulse returns before the tune
transitions.how: The calm of “Et lux perpetua luceat eis” (letter G) fades with a single horn chord. At letter H the tempo returns to Moderato and the plucked ostinato of the opening restarts in the strings, with quiet repeated notes in the timpani, while the choir is still finishing “luceat eis”. Fauré brings back the movement’s first pulse before its first melody: the rhythm that carried the baritone’s opening is heard again, and the tune has not yet returned.
transitions.evidence: The report finds a boundary at 2:52 (0.62) and onset density rising from 1.2 per second at 2:50 to 3.0 at 3:00. Pages 104–105 of the score give the horn chord at letter G and the Moderato marking at letter H, with pizzicato strings and repeated notes in the timpani staff under the choir’s last “luceat eis”.

transitions.title: The pulse thins; the choir takes the tune
transitions.how: After about nine bars of the ostinato, the choir sings the movement’s opening melody, “Libera me, Domine, de morte aeterna”, in unison. What the baritone sang alone at the start is now the whole choir’s line. The timpani’s regular pulse breaks into isolated notes and rests as the melody begins, the strings continue with repeated chords, and quiet horn and trombone chords come and go beneath. The return joins the same pulse and the same tune, now sung by many.
transitions.evidence: Pages 105–107 of the score give nine bars of ostinato after letter H, then the unison “Libera me” on page 107 with the timpani reduced to isolated notes and rests on pages 107–109 and horn and trombone chords on pages 106–109. At about two seconds a bar this puts the entry near 3:10, where the report’s onset density dips to 0.8 per second; the timing describes the whole join.

transitions.title: Baritone and choir close, pianissimo
transitions.how: The choir’s “Quando caeli movendi sunt” crescendo reaches forte, then falls away at letter L. The baritone, silent since the choir took over the text, returns alone with “Libera me, Domine, de morte aeterna”, over repeated pianissimo chords in the strings and organ. The choir answers pianissimo, and the movement ends on a bowed chord with fermatas. The soloist who began the movement closes it, with the choir’s fear now a whisper.
transitions.evidence: The report finds a boundary at 4:14 (0.44), with level falling from −13.2 dB at 4:10 to −21.3 dB at 4:15. Pages 111–113 of the score mark dim. at letter L, the baritone’s return on page 112 and the final pp choir and arco chord.

timeline.note: Pizzicato cellos and basses repeat the ostinato under the baritone; the organ holds long notes.
Violins and violas add held chords above the plucked bass.
The choir enters pianissimo in four parts with the strings and organ; the baritone rests.
Fortissimo horn chords break in at the Più mosso.
Trombones join the horns, choir and strings in the fortissimo Dies irae.
The choir sings Requiem aeternam piano and dolce; horns and trombones drop to piano.
The ostinato returns in the plucked strings, with the timpani on the rhythm, under the choir’s last luceat eis.
Quiet horn and trombone chords begin under the ostinato.
The choir sings the opening melody in unison; the timpani now play only isolated notes, not a continuous ostinato.
The baritone returns alone over repeated pianissimo chords; the choir answers and the strings end on a held chord.

fields.label: Performers
fields.value: Bernard Kruysen (baritone), Chorale Philippe Caillard (chorus), Orchestre national de l’Opéra de Monte-Carlo (orchestra), Louis Frémaux (conductor), Henri Carol (organ)
fields.note: Commons lists Bernard Kruysen and Denis Thilliez among the artists of the complete recording; Kruysen is the baritone soloist here (the sleeve credits “Bernard Kruysen, baryton”). Denis Thilliez has no part in this movement.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: Full-orchestra version, as published by Éditions Hamelle (1901)
fields.note: The sleeve credits “Editions Hamelle – Paris” and describes the version heard as the one with the more extended symphonic forces, which it says Fauré transcribed around 1899; Hamelle published the full-orchestra score in 1901. The sleeve names no editor or corrections, and the forces were not checked by ear against the score. Wikipedia notes that the 1900 autograph does not survive and that critics have asked who scored it, so authorship of the orchestration is not asserted here. The orchestra panel uses the Kalmus reprint of the Hamelle score.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: The scanned Erato sleeve prints “Enregistré … à Monaco, le 11 Août 1962”. The Commons date field (“10 August 1962”), IMSLP and René Gagnaux give 10 August 1962; Commons does not say whether its date is a session or an issue date. The 1988 CD reissue notes “Recording: 08/1962”. Both candidate days fall in 1962; the rights assessment relies on that year only.

fields.label: Place
fields.value: Cathedral of Our Lady Immaculate (Notre-Dame-de-l’Immaculée-Conception), Monaco
fields.note: The sleeve gives the cathedral in Monaco, and a 1983 Erato LP pressing (EF 28002) is noted on Discogs as “Registered in 1962 in the Cathedral of Monaco”. IMSLP and Gagnaux give the Salle Alcazar, Monte-Carlo. Commons gives no venue. The sleeve also credits the engineer: “Prise de son : Peter Willemoes”.

fields.note: No matrix or take numbers appear in the sources consulted. The sleeve lays out this movement as face 2, track 2 of the LP (face 1: Introït et Kyrie, Offertoire, Sanctus, Pie Jesu; face 2: Agnus Dei, Libera me, In paradisum, then the Cantique de Jean Racine).

fields.label: Transfer date
fields.note: The Commons upload date (23 May 2018) is not a transfer date.

fields.label: Processing
fields.note: No source-transfer or restoration processing is disclosed. Contrapunctus’ own analysis estimates the reference pitch of this movement about 40 to 60 cents above A = 440 Hz (+50 cents (CQT histogram) and +0.49 semitone (librosa estimate_tuning)); all seven movements of the set give a similar offset. Whether it comes from the orchestra’s tuning, the disc speed or the transfer speed is not established, and Hz and note names in the analysis report are not corrected for it.

fields.value: Territorial: sound recording in the public domain in the European Union (Commons PD-EU-audio; first published before 1963).
fields.note: Commons applies {{PD-EU-audio}} alone to this file (wikitext inspected at the cited revision; source “Erato Records”, date field 1962-08-10). The BnF catalogue records legal deposit in 1962 (“1962 (DL)”) for both Erato issues, LDE 3228 and STE 50128: that is the best primary evidence found that first publication came before 1963, so the 50-year EU term had expired before the term extension applied to recordings still protected on 1 November 2013 (Directive 2011/77/EU, Article 1(3)). Legal deposit is not an exact publication date and no issue month was found. The “℗ Erato Disques S.A. 1963” line on the 1988 CD reissue (ECD 40006) belongs to that reissue and is not taken as the date of first publication. A recording or session date is not used as a publication date. This is territorial and does not establish US sound-recording status.

composer.epithet: A church organist who made the French song and the chamber ensemble laboratories for harmony.
facts: École Niedermeyer, 1854–65; piano with Camille Saint-Saëns
Madeleine: choirmaster 1877–96, organist 1896–1905 · Paris Conservatoire: composition professor 1896–1905, director 1905–20
Mélodies, piano music, chamber music, Requiem, the opera Pénélope
composer.background:
Fauré learned his trade in a school for church musicians. His father was a schoolmaster in the Ariège; at nine, Gabriel was sent to Louis Niedermeyer’s recently founded school in Paris, where plainchant, Renaissance polyphony, organ playing and counterpoint belonged to the ordinary curriculum. The education matters to the harmony. A melody can cadence in minor with an unsharpened seventh degree; a chord can emerge from the independent movement of voices. These possibilities were practical knowledge before they became a recognisable Fauré style.

After Niedermeyer died in 1861, Camille Saint-Saëns took over the piano class and introduced the pupils to Schumann, Liszt and Wagner. Teacher and pupil remained friends for more than sixty years. Fauré’s graduation work, the Cantique de Jean Racine of 1865, already joins the two educations: a flowing keyboard accompaniment beneath a choral texture whose entries are controlled by contrapuntal discipline. Its French text is Racine’s paraphrase of a Latin hymn. The bass supports long phrases that carry the upper voices across the bar-lines.
